extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the MPEP/October 2019 PEG framework to determine whether patent claims are statutory and not directed to judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural products, abstract ideas), using the Step 1 / Step 2A (Prong One & Two) / Step 2B analysis and related claim-interpretation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim falls within a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter) under MPEP 2106.03.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to claim language; determine whether the claim recites a machine, manufacture, composition, or process (e.g., controller = manufacture/machine). If yes, Step 1 = YES and proceed to judicial-exception analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim recites a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim 'recites' or 'sets forth' a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea) as explained in MPEP 2106.04(II) and the October 2019 Update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify claim limitations that embody mathematical concepts, mental processes, laws of nature, or nature-based product limitations. Recitation can be explicit functional language (e.g., 'calculate using the Arrhenius equation') and multiple exceptions in a claim are permissible; if any judicial exception is recited, proceed to further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites a nature-based product limitation, analyze whether the claimed nature-based product possesses markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart (MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the analysis to the nature-based product as claimed; for mixtures/combination products, apply to the resultant combination rather than component parts. If components do not occur together in nature, compare the claimed mixture to its individual components. Consider changed structure or changed functional properties (a changed function can evidence markedly different characteristics). If markedly different characteristics exist, the product is not a 'product of nature' exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply markedly different characteristics to resultant combinations (mixtures)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nature-based products produced by combining multiple components, evaluate the resultant nature-based combination's characteristics rather than separately evaluating each component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If components don't naturally occur together, compare mixture to individual components; determine if mixing changes structure or produces new functional properties (e.g., altered glycemic control profile) that are markedly different from natural counterparts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must define the invention; unclaimed characteristics not counted
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the claimed limitation itself defines the invention and that only characteristics recited or encompassed within the BRI of the claim can contribute to eligibility (In re Roslin, Roche Molecular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify characteristics by what is recited in the claim and its BRI. The claim need not explicitly recite a markedly different characteristic so long as the BRI of the claim reflects the claimed product possesses at least one appropriate markedly different characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple recited judicial exceptions into a single exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites a series of steps or multiple limitations that each embody judicial exceptions, treat the combined recited judicial exceptions as a single judicial exception for further analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP 2106.04 and 2106.05(II) and October 2019 Update guidance; consolidation simplifies Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole 'integrates' the recited judicial exception into a practical application by (a) identifying additional elements beyond the exception and (b) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine if they integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not consider whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional at this prong. Determine if additional limitations meaningfully apply the exception to effect a practical application (e.g., improvements to technology, specific physical steps rather than mere field-linking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that merely gather data, are recited at a high level of generality, or merely instruct the application of the judicial exception (e.g., generic controller) are 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and do not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify elements that are necessary to use the exception but are described in purely conventional or high-level terms (e.g., 'repeatedly obtain measurements of temperature'). Such elements should be treated as insignificant in Step 2A Prong Two; they may be re-evaluated at Step 2B for conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality/tangibility is not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere physical/tangible nature of an additional element (e.g., a controller or device) does not by itself render a claim eligible or integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have made clear that mere physicality is not relevant; examiners should analyze the role and specificity of physical elements rather than their mere presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' / inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole amounts to 'significantly more' than the recited judicial exception by identifying an inventive concept in the additional elements individually or in combination (MPEP 2106.05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-assess elements previously deemed insignificant extra-solution activity for whether they are well-understood, routine, conventional (Berkheimer). If additional elements are well-known and generic, they will not supply 'significantly more'. Conversely, specific unconventional tools or meaningful improvements to technology can provide 'significantly more'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection practice note: explain exception and insufficiency of additional elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101, the examiner should identify the exception by pointing to specific claim limitations and explain why they describe an abstract idea/other exception, and explain why additional elements fail to integrate or amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on the conclusion that an additional element is well-understood, routine, conventional (Berkheimer Option 1), the rejection should cite support for that conclusion in the specification or other record evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements-to-technology and 'other meaningful limitations' consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: To find that a claim 'integrates' an exception by virtue of an improvement to technology or other meaningful limitations, there must be a technical explanation in the specification and the claim must reflect the asserted improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate specification and claim together; do not perform improvements analysis with reference to whether claim elements are conventional (that is excluded at Step 2A Prong Two). Examiners are not expected to make qualitative judgments on the merits of an asserted improvement except where a person of ordinary skill would clearly understand the claim/specification do not show an improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation under Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claim terms under the BRI standard consistent with the specification (MPEP 2111); preambles do not limit claims unless the preamble supplies a positive limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same claim interpretation across eligibility and other patentability requirements. When a limitation is drafted as 35 U.S.C. 112(f) means-plus-function, apply the appropriate three-prong test and corresponding-structure limitation to BRI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation satisfies the three-prong test for 112(f), its BRI is limited to the structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification and equivalents (MPEP 2181).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When 112(f) applies, the limitation will be interpreted as limited to the disclosed corresponding structure (e.g., ARCXY thermocouple) and that interpretation should be used for eligibility, novelty, obviousness, and other analyses; prior art must show the same structure or equivalents to anticipate or render obvious the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying mathematical concepts and mental processes as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical calculations, conversions, and relationships (e.g., solving Arrhenius equation; converting decimal α to percentage) can be abstract ideas and/or mental processes under the PEG and case law (e.g., Benson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such calculations may also be laws of nature if they embody natural relationships; determine whether recited calculations are simple enough to be practically performed in the human mind and whether they are merely mathematical/formulaic, which supports treating them as judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic controller or computing element does not negate mental nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting a controller or computer as the tool to perform an otherwise mental process or abstract idea does not negate the mental/abstract nature of the limitation if the controller is recited only generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A generic controller recited without structural detail typically amounts to instructions to 'apply it' on a computer and will not integrate the exception into a practical application. Specific, unconventional tools or how they are used may alter this conclusion.
